nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Chaparral shrubs grow in open, sunny, dry slopes; sunlight drives all plant growth in the park.

nodes.name: Winter rain
nodes.desc: Rain falls mostly in the cooler months. Creeks in the park do not flow all year, so water is scarce for much of it.

nodes.name: Fire
nodes.desc: Fire has long shaped the park, from lightning and from Native American burning, and keeps chaparral renewing.

nodes.name: Soil & nutrients
nodes.desc: Thin, rocky soils on volcanic rock. Nutrients return to them as dead plants and animals are broken down.

nodes.name: Soil decomposers
nodes.desc: Fungi, bacteria and soil invertebrates break down dead leaves, wood and carcasses and return nutrients to the soil.

nodes.name: Chamise
nodes.desc: A fire-adapted shrub that makes up much of the park chaparral. Wikipedia says it resprouts from its base after fire and its seeds germinate after burns.

nodes.name: Bigberry manzanita
nodes.desc: A chaparral shrub with berry-like fruit. Wikipedia says its seeds need exposure to fire before they germinate.

nodes.name: California buckwheat
nodes.desc: A common flowering shrub of the park with nectar-rich blooms and seeds, visited by bees and butterflies.

nodes.name: Western honey bee
nodes.desc: The best-recorded bee here. A 1990s census counted about 450 bee species in the park, most of them solitary, a very high density.

nodes.name: Moths & butterflies
nodes.desc: Caterpillars eat shrub leaves and adults take nectar from flowers. Moths are the main prey of Townsend's big-eared bats.

nodes.name: Narrow-faced kangaroo rat
nodes.desc: A nocturnal seed-eating rodent of chaparral slopes, and an important prey animal for snakes, cats and canids.

nodes.name: California ground squirrel
nodes.desc: Mostly eats seeds, nuts and fruit, plus some insects. Rattlesnakes are its most frequent predators.

nodes.name: Black-tailed jackrabbit
nodes.desc: A large hare that browses shrubs and grasses in open country and is eaten by coyotes and bobcats.

nodes.name: California Quail
nodes.desc: A ground-living bird that feeds on seeds, leaves and berries, and is hunted by hawks, snakes and cats.

nodes.name: Western Fence Lizard
nodes.desc: A common lizard of rocks and brush that eats insects and other small invertebrates.

nodes.name: Townsend's big-eared bat
nodes.desc: Wikipedia says it feeds almost entirely on moths. Pinnacles lists it as breeding in its talus caves, which close during pupping season.

nodes.name: Northern Pacific rattlesnake
nodes.desc: An ambush predator of rodents. Ground squirrels are among its most frequent prey.

nodes.name: Common raven
nodes.desc: An omnivore and scavenger that eats carrion, insects, eggs and small animals.

nodes.name: Turkey vulture
nodes.desc: A carrion eater that soars over the park and cleans up dead animals.

nodes.name: California condor
nodes.desc: A scavenger released at Pinnacles from 2003. Lead from ammunition in carcasses is the main cause of death for wild adults.

nodes.name: Prairie falcon
nodes.desc: Nests on cliff ledges, and Pinnacles has some of the highest breeding densities in North America. Hunts ground squirrels and birds.

nodes.name: Bobcat
nodes.desc: A solitary cat that hunts rabbits, rodents and birds across chaparral and woodland.

nodes.name: Coyote
nodes.desc: A flexible predator of rabbits, rodents and other small animals; it also scavenges.
